Start with how common flu is (prior p = 50%). Then combine true detections (TPR) and false alarms (FPR) to find the posterior probability P(flu | test +).

Bayes’ theorem in 3 natural steps: from 1,000 people to your chance of flu

The easiest way to understand Bayes’ theorem is with 1,000 people: first split them by how common flu is (p = 50%), next count how many from each row get a Test +, and finally take the sick share of all positive tests (P(flu | test +)).

Why the 1,000-person count formula equals Bayes’ formula

The vertical bar | means “given” (which group we restrict our attention to). Because TP = 1,000 × TPR × p and FP = 1,000 × FPR × (1 − p), the population size 1,000 cancels out from top and bottom—turning expected counts into Bayes’ exact rate formula for P(flu | test +).

0.96 × 0.5 ÷ [0.96 × 0.5 + 0.04 × 0.5] = 96%

Positive Likelihood Ratio (LR+ = TPR ÷ FPR): 24×. Dividing TP by FP gives Posterior Odds = LR+ × Prior Odds.
